builder_plan.scenario: A narrow, repeated product task may not need your largest model.
builder_plan.change: Check whether a released student model fits the task before generating training data.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current model and an off-the-shelf small model on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Student quality, serving cost, teacher calls, training cost, and failures on unusual inputs.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: CoRD: Coupled Rollouts Fill the Blind Spot of On-Policy Distillation
summary: CoRD replaces the state distribution of standard on-policy distillation: instead of training the student purely on its own rollouts, it draws training states from a geometric interpolation of student and teacher via the maximal coupling of speculative decoding, substituting teacher tokens only where the student underweights the target. The cost is that both student and teacher distributions must be evaluated token-by-token during rollout generation (the same machinery as speculative decoding), adding teacher inference passes to data generation and implementation complexity, though interventions recede as the student improves. It can fail if the reader's pipeline relies on third-party APIs that do not expose token-level logits for both models (the coupling requires both distributions), if no suitable teacher of the same family is available, or if the workload is not a verifiable-reasoning task where the pass@1/pass@8 gains were demonstrated.
rationale: The gains are real but modest (1-3 points), require logits-level access to both student and teacher plus a non-trivial coupled-sampling implementation, and are validated only on math reasoning with Qwen-family models, so a small team should validate it on their own distillation workload before committing.

claims.statement: CoRD replaces the state distribution of standard on-policy distillation: instead of training the student purely on its own rollouts, it draws training states from a geometric interpolation of student and teacher via the maximal coupling of speculative decoding, substituting teacher tokens only where the student underweights the target. The cost is that both student and teacher distributions must be evaluated token-by-token during rollout generation (the same machinery as speculative decoding), adding teacher inference passes to data generation and implementation complexity, though interventions recede as the student improves. It can fail if the reader's pipeline relies on third-party APIs that do not expose token-level logits for both models (the coupling requires both distributions), if no suitable teacher of the same family is available, or if the workload is not a verifiable-reasoning task where the pass@1/pass@8 gains were demonstrated.

Across six Qwen3/Qwen3.5 students (0.6B-4B) on five math benchmarks, CoRD raises average pass@1 over on-policy distillation by 0.9 to 2.0 points and pass@8 by 1.2 to 3.4 points at equal training steps and data; on frozen teacher-reached states, a 4B student reaches in 16 steps a gap closure that plain on-policy distillation does not reach in 80.
